outline.chapter_title: 1. The FOIA Request, the FBI File, and the Litigation’s Procedural Path
outline.description: This chapter introduces the factual setting and procedural history that frame the dispute. It explains who Farahi is, why his FBI file mattered, how the FBI responded to his FOIA request, and how the district court managed the case over time, including its insistence on updated declarations before granting summary judgment.

outline.chapter_title: 2. The Governing FOIA Framework: Exemption 7(A), Segregability, and Standards of Review
outline.description: This chapter sets out the legal architecture the D.C. Circuit applied. It explains FOIA’s general disclosure rule, the elements of Exemption 7(A), the requirement that enforcement proceedings be pending or reasonably anticipated, the separate duty to segregate nonexempt information, and the evidentiary and appellate standards governing review.

outline.chapter_title: 3. Why the File Was 'Compiled for Law Enforcement Purposes'
outline.description: This chapter explains the first Exemption 7(A) element and why it was easily satisfied here. It walks through the nexus requirement for law-enforcement records, the deference owed to the FBI, and the court’s reliance on both the public and ex parte declarations, as well as Farahi’s own concessions about the subject matter of the investigation.

outline.chapter_title: 4. Interference with Pending or Reasonably Anticipated Enforcement Proceedings
outline.description: This chapter covers the core dispute in the appeal: whether the FBI adequately showed that disclosure could interfere with enforcement proceedings that remained live. It explains the court’s treatment of the Hardy and Bender declarations, Farahi’s staleness and conclusoriness objections, the importance of context, and the court’s reliance on public and sealed materials to find an ongoing concrete proceeding.

outline.chapter_title: 5. Segregability, Ex Parte Review, and the Case’s Final Disposition
outline.description: This chapter explains the final step in the court’s analysis: even when Exemption 7(A) applies, the agency must still release reasonably segregable nonexempt information. It details why the court accepted the FBI’s position that no meaningful information could be segregated, how it justified reliance on ex parte submissions, and how these conclusions led to affirmance.
